name: Ara-290

lead: ARA 290 (cibinetide) is a short peptide derived from erythropoietin, designed to trigger tissue-protective signalling without boosting red blood cells. Recovery-focused users discuss it for tissue protection and nerve healing.

It is designed to activate the innate repair receptor, which researchers describe as mediating tissue protection and anti-inflammation, while avoiding the hematologic effects of EPO. Small exploratory trials in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes neuropathy reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements.

paras: It is investigational and has no approved use. In peptide communities it is discussed as a repair-oriented compound for recovery, though human data come from small patient trials rather than healthy trainees.
Safety data come from small patient trials. It is investigational with no approved use, and its effects in healthy people have not been studied.

angle.text: ARA 290 is an EPO-derived peptide that activates a tissue repair receptor, and recovery-focused users discuss it for faster tissue healing and better recovery between sessions. It has been tested in small neuropathy trials in sarcoidosis and diabetes.

lead: ARA 290, also known as cibinetide, is an 11-amino-acid peptide engineered from the structure of erythropoietin (EPO). It was designed to activate the innate repair receptor involved in tissue protection without raising red blood cell counts, avoiding the thrombosis risk associated with recombinant EPO.[1][2][3]

It was developed by Araim Pharmaceuticals and has been tested in small human trials of neuropathic symptoms in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes.[4][5][6] Authors of these studies reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements, but the trials were small and exploratory.[5][6][2] No study of ARA 290 for appearance was found.

paras: Researchers describe a tissue-protection system mediated by locally produced hyposialated EPO that activates an innate repair receptor, triggered by cellular stress. Recombinant EPO is limited for this purpose by rises in hematocrit and platelet activation; ARA 290 was engineered to activate the repair receptor without these effects.[1][3] Preclinical studies reported long-term relief of neuropathic pain with suppression of the spinal microglia response, and protection of transplanted islets in animal models.[7][8]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study enrolled 22 sarcoidosis patients with symptoms of small fibre neuropathy, giving ARA 290 three times weekly, and was published in 2012.[5] A 2013 report described improved symptoms and increased corneal nerve fibre density in sarcoidosis patients with small nerve fibre loss.[6] A larger Phase 2 trial in sarcoidosis neuropathy (about 64 participants) was registered in 2014.[9]

A 2015 study in patients with type 2 diabetes and painful neuropathy reported improved metabolic control and neuropathic symptoms.[2] A registered Phase 2 trial in prediabetes and type 2 diabetes enrolled 24 participants,[10] and a Phase 2 trial in diabetic macular oedema was terminated after about 9 participants.[11] A review summarised the clinical development in sarcoidosis neuropathy.[3]
No studies were found of ARA 290 in healthy people or for cosmetic, recovery or performance outcomes.
The published pilot studies describe the peptide as tested for safety alongside efficacy, in small groups. Long-term and large-scale safety data are not available in the sources reviewed.[5][2]
